newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: VNU PLANS TO EXPAND IN MARKETING INFO.
newsitem.headline: VNU PLANS TO EXPAND IN MARKETING INFO.

text.p: Dutch publisher VNU said on Tuesday international expansion in marketing information services (MIS) was one of its strategic priorities.
"We will certainly invest a lot in (MIS) in the coming years and we expect to see a lot of growth in this area," VNU chairman Joep Brentjens told a news conference.
But VNU would also invest to defend its strong market position in the Dutch magazine and regional newspaper markets and it had no plans to withdraw from commercial TV, he said.
Marketing information forms part of VNU's business information operations in the U.S. and Europe which posted profit growth of 45.9 and 43.2 percent respectively last year.
Business information as a whole generated 43 percent of VNU's operating profits in 1996, up from seven percent in 1992.
"This is the growth area for VNU. That is what we saw last year and we expect it to remain so," finance manager Frans Cremers said.
Brentjens said demand for VNU's marketing information services for advertisers, advertising agencies and media groups was growing strongly in the United States.
From its strong U.S. base VNU now planned to expand nto other regions. "We plan to start operating worldwide in marketing information services," Brentjens said.
VNU's 1995 acquisition of British demographic marketing data firm Calyx formed part of this plan and Calyx was currently expanding gradually into continental Europe, he said.
There were also plans to start selling services worldwide under the name of Claritas, VNU's U.S. geodemographic market research unit, Brentjens said.
These international expansion plans included the Far East and Asia, he said, where VNU took a 26 percent stake in marketing research and marketing data firm Org Marg last month.

Brentjens said big producers of branded consumer products such as Unilever, Prcter & Gamble and Nestle were keen to buy similar marketing information services from VNU in other countries to those they bought in the United States.
As the methods and techniques involved were the same, it was mainly a question of acquiring local market data, he said.
Brentjens said VNU would probably also expand selectively in some areas of trade and professional magazine publishing and in consumer magazines in Eastern Europe.

In the Netherlands VNU would defend its traditionally strong position in consumer magazines and regional newspapers, for example by taking part in regional television projects through its newspapers, he said.
Despite the complete erosion of TV profits in 1996 due to fierce competition, Brentjens said VNU did not plan to withdraw from commercial television in the Netherlands and Belgium.
As the leading channels in the Dutch and Belgian markets respectively, RTL4 and VTM were well placed to benefit from a recovery in the television advertising market, he said.
However, Brentjens said margins were unlikely to be as high as a few years ago when RTL4 ruled the roost as the only commercial television station in the Netherlands.
In the Netherlands VNU has pooled its 38 percent stake in the RTL4 and RTL5 channels with the Veronica channel in a joint venture known as Holland Media Group (HMG).
